## Overview

A generation is the composite
`develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ record ⋅ rescale ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap`
([The categorical layer](../05_categorical_layer/05_categorical_layer.qmd)); the variants
below leave out `record` and `rescale`, which would do nothing in them. Because each
step is a value, the model can be changed by changing the composite: replacing a step,
dropping one, repeating one, inserting a new one, or stratifying the population into
demes. The validated kernel functions are reused unchanged in every variant below; only
the wiring differs.

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
import Catlab                       # loads QTLSim's categorical layer
using Catlab: ⋅, ⊗
using CairoMakie, Printf, Random, Statistics
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
(; develop, select, reproduce, mutate, swap, generation) = operators()
nothing
```

`run!` runs the standard generation, and `run_composed` runs a life cycle written as
syntax ([One life cycle, two backends](../07_one_life_cycle_two_backends/07_one_life_cycle_two_backends.qmd)).
For operators composed directly, as here, we write a small driver that runs any
composite and records the mean phenotype and genetic variance of the parents each
generation. Recording calls `develop!`, which uses no random numbers, so it does not
disturb the run.

```{julia}
function run_variant(genop, p::Params; seed)
    rng = Xoshiro(seed); w = World(p)
    w.env .= sqrt(envVar(p)) .* randn(rng, p.PopSize)
    gens = Int[]; zbar = Float64[]; vg = Float64[]; θ = Float64[]
    for g in 0:p.NoGenerations-1
        w.gen = g
        develop!(w)
        push!(gens, g); push!(zbar, mean(w.phenotype)); push!(vg, var(w.genotype)); push!(θ, w.θ)
        genop(w, rng)
        w.extinct && break
    end
    (gen = gens, pheno_mean = zbar, geno_var = vg, theta = θ, extinct = w.extinct)
end

base = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 1, NoGenerations = 2000,
              PhenotypeVar = 0.02, Heritability = 0.5, MutationScalar = 0.02,
              MutationRatePerGamete = 0.5, InitFitnessSD = 0.3)
colours = [:navy, :teal, :crimson]
nothing
```

## Replacing the selection operator

`select` is one link of the chain. Replacing it changes the selection regime while
reproduction and mutation stay the same. Two alternatives: neutral drift, in which
everyone survives, and truncation selection, in which only the top fifth of the
population by phenotype breeds.

```{julia}
drift = operator(:drift, function (w, rng)
    fill!(w.fitness, 1.0)
    resize!(w.survivors, w.p.PopSize); w.survivors .= 1:w.p.PopSize
    w.nsurv = w.p.PopSize
    w
end)

truncation(frac) = operator(:truncation, function (w, rng)
    k = max(2, round(Int, frac * w.p.PopSize))
    top = partialsortperm(w.phenotype, 1:k; rev = true)
    resize!(w.survivors, k); w.survivors .= top; w.nsurv = k
    w
end)

selection_variants = [
    ("stabilising", develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap),
    ("drift", develop ⋅ drift ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap),
    ("truncation (top 20%)", develop ⋅ truncation(0.2) ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap),
]
runs1 = [(name, run_variant(g, base; seed = 1)) for (name, g) in selection_variants]
nothing
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-selection
#| fig-cap: "Replacing only the selection operator. Left: stabilising selection holds the mean at the optimum, drift lets it wander, and truncation selection drives it steadily upward. Right: genetic variance reaches a mutation–selection balance under stabilising selection, builds up under drift and is depleted by truncation."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "mean phenotype")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "genetic variance")
for ((name, r), c) in zip(runs1, colours)
    lines!(ax1, r.gen, r.pheno_mean, color = c, label = name)
    lines!(ax2, r.gen, r.geno_var, color = c, label = name)
end
axislegend(ax1, position = :lt)
fig
```

## Dropping or repeating mutation

Leaving `mutate` out lets selection and drift use up the variance; composing it twice
doubles the mutational input, and the balance rises.

```{julia}
mutation_variants = [
    ("no mutation", develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ swap),
    ("mutation", develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap),
    ("mutation twice", develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap),
]
runs2 = [(name, run_variant(g, base; seed = 2)) for (name, g) in mutation_variants]
for (name, r) in runs2
    @printf("%-15s mean genetic variance over the last 500 generations: %.5f\n",
            name, mean(r.geno_var[end-499:end]))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mutation
#| fig-cap: "Changing the mutation input by recomposition. Without mutation the genetic variance decays; with mutation applied twice per generation the balance is higher than with the standard generation."
fig = Figure(size = (640, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "genetic variance")
for ((name, r), c) in zip(runs2, colours)
    lines!(ax, r.gen, r.geno_var, color = c, label = name)
end
axislegend(ax, position = :rt)
fig
```

## Inserting a new operator: a fluctuating optimum

New biology can be added as a new operator, built with `operator(name, act)`. In QTSim the optimum either stands still or
moves at a constant rate; here an operator sets it to oscillate,
$\theta_t = A \sin(2\pi t / P)$, and is inserted before selection. (`select` only moves
the optimum itself when `MoveFitnessSDGen` is set, so it leaves this one alone.)

```{julia}
fluctuating(A, P) = operator(:fluctuate, (w, rng) -> (w.θ = A * sin(2π * w.gen / P); w))

periods = [20, 100, 500]
runs3 = [(P, run_variant(develop ⋅ fluctuating(0.1, P) ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap,
                         base; seed = 3)) for P in periods]
for (P, r) in runs3
    late = length(r.gen)-999:length(r.gen)
    @printf("period %3d: the mean phenotype follows the optimum with correlation %.2f\n",
            P, cor(r.pheno_mean[late], r.theta[late]))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-fluctuating
#| fig-cap: "A population under an optimum oscillating with amplitude 0.1 (dashed) and three periods. It tracks slow oscillations closely, lags behind intermediate ones and responds only weakly to fast ones."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 300))
for (k, (P, r)) in enumerate(runs3)
    ax = Axis(fig[1, k], title = "period $P", xlabel = "generation",
              ylabel = k == 1 ? "phenotype / optimum" : "", limits = ((1000, 2000), (-0.15, 0.15)))
    lines!(ax, r.gen, r.theta, color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
    lines!(ax, r.gen, r.pheno_mean, color = colours[k])
end
fig
```

## Stratifying with ⊗ and coupling with migration

`⊗` turns one population into a metapopulation of demes, and the composed generation
acts on each deme. A `migration` operator composed in with `⋅` couples them. Under
neutral drift, isolated demes drift apart; a little migration keeps them together.

```{julia}
function run_demes(genop, s, ngen; seed)
    rng = Xoshiro(seed)
    for d in s.demes; d.env .= sqrt(envVar(d.p)) .* randn(rng, d.p.PopSize); end
    means = [Float64[] for _ in s.demes]
    for g in 0:ngen-1
        for (k, d) in enumerate(s.demes)
            d.gen = g; develop!(d); push!(means[k], mean(d.phenotype))
        end
        genop(s, rng)
    end
    means
end

small = Params(PopSize = 200, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 1, PhenotypeVar = 0.02, Heritability = 0.5,
               MutationScalar = 0.05, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.5)
neutral = develop ⋅ drift ⋅ reproduce ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap
isolated = run_demes(neutral, small ⊗ demes(4), 2500; seed = 4)
coupled = run_demes(neutral ⋅ migration(0.05), small ⊗ demes(4), 2500; seed = 4)
spread(ms) = std([m[end] for m in ms])
@printf("spread of the deme means after 2500 generations: isolated %.3f, with migration %.3f\n",
        spread(isolated), spread(coupled))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-demes
#| fig-cap: "Four neutral demes. Left: isolated, their means drift apart. Right: with 5% migration per generation composed into the generation, they stay together."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "deme mean phenotype", title = "isolated")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", title = "with migration")
for k in 1:4
    lines!(ax1, 0:length(isolated[k])-1, isolated[k], color = (:teal, 0.8))
    lines!(ax2, 0:length(coupled[k])-1, coupled[k], color = (:crimson, 0.8))
end
linkyaxes!(ax1, ax2)
fig
```

## Steps with parameters: demes under different selection

The operators above take their parameters from `Params`. A step of the life cycle can
carry its own instead, as part of the syntax: `withparams` gives a step parameters, and
the result is a new generator, named by the step and its parameters, with the same type.
Here deme 1 selects toward an optimum of 0.1 with width 0.3, and deme 2 toward −0.1 with
width 0.15. `migrate(2; rate)` carries its rate.

```{julia}
L = lifecycle(); g = L.generation
narrow = withparams(L.select; θ = -0.1, ω = 0.15)
println(narrow, ": ", Catlab.dom(narrow), " → ", Catlab.codom(narrow))
two_demes(rate) = withparams(g; θ = 0.1, ω = 0.3) ⊗ withparams(g; θ = -0.1, ω = 0.15) ⋅ L.migrate(2; rate)
two_demes(0.01)
```

The same life cycle lowers to the kernel and to the moments of a Gaussian population, and
each step's parameters go with it. In the moments lowering, `migrate` mixes the demes as
the kernel's migration does: a deme's mean becomes the weighted mean of the demes its
individuals came from, and its genetic variance the variance within them plus the
variance between their means. Below, 20 kernel runs per migration rate are averaged and
set against the moments.

```{julia}
pd = Params(base; PopSize = 500, NoGenerations = 1000)
rates = [0.0, 0.005, 0.02]
deme(o, d) = (i = findall(==(d), o.deme); (o.gen[i], o.pheno_mean[i], o.geno_var[i]))
moments = [run_moments(pd; cycle = two_demes(r)) for r in rates]
kernel = map(rates) do r
    runs = [run_composed(pd ⊗ demes(2), Xoshiro(s); cycle = two_demes(r)) for s in 1:20]
    [mean(deme(o, d)[k] for o in runs) for d in 1:2, k in 2:3]   # mean trajectories
end
for (r, mo, k) in zip(rates, moments, kernel)
    late(x) = mean(x[601:end])
    @printf("rate %.3f: deme means differ by %.3f in the kernel, %.3f in the moments\n",
            r, late(k[1, 1]) - late(k[2, 1]), late(deme(mo, 1)[2]) - late(deme(mo, 2)[2]))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-step-parameters
#| fig-cap: "Two demes selected toward different optima (dashed), deme 2 more narrowly, at three migration rates. Kernel means over 20 runs (solid) and the moments lowering (dotted). Migration pulls the deme means together, and more strongly the deme under weaker selection. Right: genetic variance, which migration raises in both demes."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "deme mean phenotype")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "genetic variance")
hlines!(ax1, [0.1, -0.1], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
for (r, mo, k, c) in zip(rates, moments, kernel, colours), d in 1:2
    gens = deme(mo, d)[1]
    lines!(ax1, gens, k[d, 1], color = c, label = d == 1 ? "rate $r" : nothing)
    lines!(ax1, gens, deme(mo, d)[2], color = c, linestyle = :dot)
    lines!(ax2, gens, k[d, 2], color = c, linestyle = d == 1 ? :solid : :dashdot)
    lines!(ax2, gens, deme(mo, d)[3], color = c, linestyle = :dot)
end
axislegend(ax1, position = :rc)
fig
```

The moments get the means right and the direction of every effect. They predict a little
less divergence under migration than the kernel shows, because this one-locus kernel holds
more genetic variance than the Gaussian approximation, as it does without migration. With
the moments lowering covering several demes, any metapopulation built from these steps has
a deterministic prediction, and each deme can have its own parameters there, in the
kernel (`[p1, p2] ⊗ demes(2)`) and in SLiM (`slim_script(cycle, [p1, p2])`).

Every variant here is a line of composition rather than a change to the simulator.
That rearranging the operators is well defined, that composition is associative and a
run is the iterate of one composed generation, is what
`lean/CategoricalQuantGen/Composition.lean` proves.
